newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvians save grim mementoes of mudslide dead.
newsitem.headline: Peruvians save grim mementoes of mudslide dead.

text.p: Bleary-eyed Gregorio Chipa Sanchez clutched a handful of family photos in his muddy hands and a bundle of clothes and papers under his arm.

"This is all I found of my brother and nephew," he said. "And this," he added, holding up a piece of scarred scalp with black hair. "I'm pretty sure this belonged to my nephew because I recognise the scar."

Chipa's brother and nephew were among the 250 to 300 people reported missing after a mountainside collapsed in Peru's southeastern Andes before dawn on Tuesday, burying two Quechua-speaking farming communities in a torrent of mud.

By late Wednesday, rescuers had recovered 41 bodies, many mutilated and disfigured by the river of mud and rocks that swept away the villages of Ccocha and Pumaranra. In the central square of nearby Kerapata, civil defence officials and forensic experts recorded details of the bodies before sending them to a makeshift morgue in a schoolhouse in the neighbouring town of Tamburco.

"This one has lacerations on both feet," medical examiner Maria Navarrete Huaman told a civil defence worker jotting down the details she dictated. "We have 41 bodies so far and some parts of bodies -- arms, legs, extremities."
Tears streamed down the cheeks of Lucio Huaylla Velasquez as the magnitude of the disaster began to sink in. He lost his wife, 7-year-old daughter and 18-month-old son.
"First, the terrorists kill us with guns and now this," he sobbed, referring to the guerrilla wars that plague Peru. "I have nothing, not even a box to bury them in. There is no justice."

From a helicopter, the landslide looked like a wide brown gash on the face of the green mountainside. Roofs of the houses of what used to be Ccocha and Pumaranra poked through mud up to 30 feet (10 metres) deep in places. At the base of the mudslide, scores of rescuers were digging for bodies.

Dressed in mourning black, Dina Rivas Tapia stared up the hill from Kerapata's town square to the landslide, handkerchief in hand. "My entire family has disappeared. They were 25 people. I have no house, no money, I don't even have a bed."

Amid the tragedy, there were also stories of narrow escapes. When 14-year-old Alejandra Huallya Quispe heard a loud rumbling, she grabbed her sister and ran out of the house. But her mother and another sister were crushed: "I jumped with my sister but the 'huayco' came and crushed my mother and other sister."

Huayco is the name people in this part of the Andes give to the mudslides that come with the rainy season. With 1-1/2 months to go before the rains end, authorities fear further torrential rains could trigger more mudslides.
